stem: A 38-year-old man with a history of alcohol dependence (abstinent for 5 years) presents with a 3-week history of progressive cognitive decline, memory loss, and ataxia. He is a known heavy drinker until age 33. MRI brain shows marked atrophy of the mammillary bodies and thalamus. He has a normal EEG. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and management?
options: Korsakoff's syndrome — high-dose IV thiamine (Pabrinex) may prevent further progression, but the cognitive deficits are likely IRREVERSIBLE; manage with cognitive support and supervision
Wernicke's encephalopathy — give IV thiamine immediately
Dementa with Lewy bodies — start rivastigmine
distractors_rationale: Alzheimer's typically has a different MRI pattern (hippocampal, posterior temporoparietal atrophy) and a more gradual course. The combination of mammillary body atrophy, history of alcohol dependence, and ataxia strongly suggests Korsakoff's syndrome.

CORRECT. KORSAKOFF'S SYNDROME is a chronic neuropsychiatric condition resulting from THIAMINE (Vitamin B1) deficiency, usually in the context of chronic alcohol dependence. It is the chronic phase of WERNICKE-KORSAKOFF SYNDROME (WKS). KEY FEATURES: (1) SEVERE ANTEROGRADE AMNESIA (inability to form new memories — the hallmark); (2) VARIABLE RETROGRADE AMNESIA; (3) CONFABULATION (making up stories to fill gaps — 'honestly lying'); (4) APATHY; (5) LACK OF INSIGHT; (6) Other cognitive functions relatively preserved (compared to Alzheimer's). PATHOLOGY: necrotic lesions in the MAMMILLARY BODIES (as seen on MRI), DORSOMEDIAL NUCLEUS OF THE THALAMUS, and periaqueductal grey. MANAGEMENT: (1) THIAMINE — high-dose IV/IM (Pabrinex) is ESSENTIAL in the ACUTE phase (Wernicke's) to PREVENT progression to Korsakoff's. ONCE KORSAKOFF'S IS ESTABLISHED, thiamine may ARREST PROGRESSION but the cognitive deficits are LARGELY IRREVERSIBLE (only about 20-30% of patients recover partially). (2) The patient is no longer drinking and presents late (age 38, 5 years abstinent) — the damage may be established. (3) MANAGEMENT: (a) Cognitive support — memory aids, prompts, supervision, residential care if needed; (b) Assess capacity to make decisions (financial, care, accommodation) — he may need a Deputyship Order; (c) Treat any residual alcohol dependence (relapse prevention); (d) Check for other vitamin deficiencies; (e) Involve occupational therapy and social care.
FTD typically presents with behavioural changes (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy) or language problems, not with the specific amnestic profile and mammillary body atrophy seen here.

Wernicke's encephalopathy is the ACUTE phase of thiamine deficiency: confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia (classic triad — only present in 30%). It is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY requiring IMMEDIATE IV thiamine. If untreated, ~80% progress to Korsakoff's syndrome. This patient presents 3 weeks into the illness — it may have started as Wernicke's and is now transitioning to Korsakoff's (which is CHRONIC and IRREVERSIBLE). The established amnesia and mammillary body atrophy suggest Korsakoff's rather than acute Wernicke's.
DLB presents with visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, Parkinsonism — none of which are described.
teaching_point: Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome — HIGH-YIELD MRCPsych: WERNICKE'S ENCEPHALOPATHY (ACUTE): Onset: sudden (hours-days). TRIAD: (1) Confusion; (2) Ataxia; (3) Ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus. Only 30% present with ALL three. MANAGEMENT: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — IV thiamine (Pabrinex) IMMEDIATELY, before any glucose (glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's). Response: rapid improvement of eye signs within hours; confusion resolves over days. KORSAKOFF'S SYNDROME (CHRONIC): Onset: after Wernicke's (untreated in ~80%). KEY FEATURES: Anterograde amnesia (hallmark), confabulation, apathy. PROGNOSIS: 20-30% partial recovery, most remain severely impaired. PREVENTION in alcohol detoxification: IV thiamine (Pabrinex) for ALL high-risk patients (heavy drinking, poor nutrition, abnormal LFTs, previous WKS). COCHRANE REVIEW: Oral thiamine is INADEQUATE for treatment of WKS — IV/IM is required. The CAGE: 'EYE OPENER' (morning drinking) → CAGE question 4. But the key: thiamine is B1, deficiency causes Wernicke's/Korsakoff's. B3 (niacin) deficiency causes pellagra (dementia, dermatitis, diarrhoea). B12 deficiency causes pernicious anaemia, neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the cord, and dementia.
source: NICE CG115: Alcohol dependence; Thomson AD et al. (2008) Wernicke-Korsakoff; BNF (Pabrinex)

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a 6-year history of progressive cognitive decline, 60-year smoking history (40/day), and hypertension presents to the memory clinic. Her daughter reports a STEPWISE decline over 2 years following a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). The patient has difficulty with planning and organisation, slowness of thinking, and urinary urgency. MMSE 24/30 (deficits in attention and clock-drawing). MRI shows extensive periventricular white matter changes and multiple lacunar infarcts. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and recommended management?
options: VASCULAR DEMENTIA — OPTIMISE CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS (BP, smoking cessation, antiplatelet, statin) and offer donepezil (limited evidence)
Dementa with Lewy bodies — start rivastigmine
Normal pressure hydrocephalus — consider lumbar puncture and VP shunt
distractors_rationale: Alzheimer's typically presents with insidious-onset, progressive short-term memory loss, not stepwise decline after TIA, and not the extensive white matter changes/small vessel ischaemia seen on MRI.

CORRECT. VASCULAR DEMENTIA (VaD) — or VASCULAR COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT. NICE NG97: 'Suspect a diagnosis of vascular dementia if the onset is acute (e.g., after a stroke), or if there is a stepwise deterioration with fluctuations, and there are focal neurological signs or vascular risk factors (hypertension, smoking, diabetes, AF).' KEY FEATURES: (1) STEPWISE decline (rather than gradual — vs Alzheimer's); (2) Prominent FRONTAL/EXECUTIVE dysfunction (planning, organising — 'subcortical' pattern); (3) BRADYPHRENIA (slow thinking/slowness of processing); (4) Urinary symptoms (urgency, incontinence) — early; (5) Focal neurological signs; (6) Gait disturbance (vascular parkinsonism). MRI: WHITE MATTER HYPERINTENSITIES (chronic small vessel disease), LACUNAR INFARCTS (basal ganglia, internal capsule, thalamus), STRATEGIC INFARCTS (thalamus, caudate, angular gyrus — can cause disproportionate cognitive impairment). CLASSIFICATION: (1) Multi-infarct dementia (large vessel cortical infarcts); (2) Subcortical ischaemic dementia / BINSWANGER'S DISEASE (small vessel disease, white matter changes — as seen here); (3) Strategic infarct dementia (single strategically placed infarct). MANAGEMENT: (1) CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTOR MANAGEMENT — THIS IS THE PRIORITY: BP control (target <130/80), smoking cessation, antiplatelet (aspirin/clopidogrel), statin, diabetes control. This can SLOW PROGRESSION and reduce risk of further strokes. (2) CHOLINESTERASE INHIBITORS: limited evidence for VaD. NICE does NOT recommend donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine for VaD (the evidence is inconsistent). HOWEVER, they may be considered if there is concomitant Alzheimer's pathology (mixed dementia). The trial data: ChEIs show marginal benefit in VaD (1 point on cognition scales) but the evidence is inferior to AD. (3) Address other risk factors: smoking cessation (the single most effective intervention for this patient). VASCULAR DEPRESSION: up to 30% of VaD patients have depression — treat with SSRIs. PROGNOSIS: variable; risk factors control can slow progression.
DLB has visual hallucinations, fluctuations, and Parkinsonism — not a stepwise decline with extensive white matter changes after TIA.
FTD presents with behavioural/personality change or language problems, not subcortical cognitive slowing and stepwise decline.

NPH presents with the classic triad: gait apraxia (magnetic gait), urinary incontinence, cognitive decline. Imaging: enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal widening. This patient has extensive white matter changes, not hydrocephalus.
teaching_point: Vascular dementia vs Alzheimer's disease — classic MRCPsych comparison: VASCULAR: Stepwise onset/deterioration, executive dysfunction > memory, bradyphrenia, focal signs, urinary symptoms, white matter changes/lacunes on MRI, early gait disturbance, depression common. ALZHEIMER'S: Insidious, gradual, memory loss >> executive dysfunction, no focal signs, hippocampal atrophy, no early gait disturbance, apathy > depression. BINSWANGER'S DISEASE: A subtype of subcortical vascular dementia: (1) Small vessel disease (hypertension, diabetes leading to lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries); (2) Periventricular white matter changes on MRI; (3) Gait disorder, urinary incontinence, emotional lability, mild cognitive impairment, bradyphrenia. (4) The 'MULTIPLE LACUNAR STATE' — a synonym. (5) More common in patients with poorly controlled hypertension and smoking. (6) Management: aggressive BP control is essential (systolic <130).
source: NICE NG97: Dementia; Roman GC et al. (2002) Subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia; BNF

Theme: Suicide Epidemiology and Risk Factors

For each statement, select the CORRECT STATISTICAL FACT:

A. 1% (lifetime risk in the UK general population)
B. 5-10% (lifetime risk in people with schizophrenia)
C. 10-15% (lifetime risk in people with bipolar disorder)
D. 10% (lifetime risk in people with borderline personality disorder)
E. 15-20% (lifetime risk in people with severe depression)
F. 3-4× (increased risk in men vs women in the UK)
G. 5-6× (increased risk in people with mental illness in prison)
H. 40% (proportion of inquests of patients who died by suicide who had contact with mental health services in the past week)
I. 25% (proportion who had contact in the past month)
J. 70-80% (proportion who had NO contact with mental health services in the past year)
options: What is the approximate LIFETIME RISK of suicide in people with MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER requiring hospitalisation?
What is the approximate LIFETIME RISK of suicide in people with BIPOLAR DISORDER?
What is the approximate lifetime risk of suicide in people with SCHIZOPHRENIA?
What proportion of people who die by suicide have had NO CONTACT with specialist mental health services in the year before death?
distractors_rationale: E — 15-20%. The lifetime suicide risk for patients with MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER who have been HOSPITALISED for depression is approximately 15-20% (some studies suggest 10-15%). For ALL patients with depression (including outpatient), the risk is around 5-10%. The key MRCPsych fact: the lifetime suicide risk in DEPRESSION is 15% (held to be the highest across the major mental illnesses). HOWEVER: recent meta-analyses suggest the risk may be lower (around 5-10%) due to better treatment. The figure of 15-20% comes from older studies of hospitalised patients with severe depression (before modern antidepressants). The current BMA/GP literature: about 1 in 10 patients with severe depression dies by suicide.

C — 10-15%. The lifetime risk in BIPOLAR DISORDER is estimated at 10-15%. Bipolar disorder carries the HIGHEST RISK of suicide of all psychiatric conditions after depression. The risk is HIGHEST DURING DEPRESSIVE EPISODES and MIXED STATES (not during mania — though irritability can increase risk). Risk factors: early onset, comorbid substance misuse, family history of suicide, previous attempts, hopelessness. Lithium is the only medication with evidence for SUICIDE PREVENTION across mood disorders (reduces risk by ~60% — Cipriani et al., 2013). The key difference: bipolar has slightly lower suicide risk than severe depression (15-20% > 10-15%) but higher than schizophrenia.

B — 5-10%. The lifetime suicide risk in SCHIZOPHRENIA is estimated at 5-10%. THAT IS HIGHER THAN THE GENERAL POPULATION (1%) BUT LOWER THAN MOOD DISORDERS (10-20%). Risk factors: younger males, early illness stage (first 5 years), high premorbid functioning (the 'insight paradox' — those with MORE insight and higher functioning appear to be at HIGHER risk), depressive symptoms, post-psychotic depression, previous attempts, substance misuse. Clozapine is the ONLY antipsychotic with FDA-approved indication for reducing suicidality in schizophrenia (the InterSePT trial, 2003 — clozapine reduced suicidal behaviour by ~25% vs olanzapine). KEY: The highest risk period is the FIRST YEAR after diagnosis and in the immediate Post-discharge period from hospital.

J — 70-80% of people who die by suicide have had NO CONTACT with specialist mental health services in the year before death (The National Confidential Inquiry into Suicide and Homicide by People with Mental Illness, University of Manchester — annual reports). This is a critical public health finding: the majority of suicides occur in people NOT under specialist mental health care. Among those who ARE under mental health care, about 40% had contact in the PAST WEEK and about 25% in the PAST MONTH. KEY FINDINGS from the NCISH: (1) Most patients who die by suicide are NOT under mental health care; (2) Among those who ARE under care, the majority are not assessed as high risk (most suicides occur in LOW or MEDIUM risk categories — risk predictability is poor); (3) Risk factors: alcohol/substance misuse, adverse life events, social isolation, recent discharge from psychiatric hospital (first 2 weeks is highest risk — ensure timely follow-up); (4) Prevention strategies: reduce access to means, improve crisis services, follow up within 48 hours of discharge, family involvement. The overall suicide rate in the UK is ~10-12 per 100,000 population. The rate in psychiatric inpatients is ~100 per 100,000.
teaching_point: Suicide epidemiology — ESSENTIAL MRCPsych facts: (1) Lifetime risk: General population ~1%, BIPD ~10-15%, Schizophrenia 5-10%, Depression (severe) 15-20%, BPD 10%, Alcohol dependence ~10%, Anorexia ~5%. (2) The 1% lifetime risk in the general population is a crucial baseline ('1 in 100 people will die by suicide'). (3) Men are 3-4× more likely to die by suicide in the UK (the 'gender paradox': women attempt more, men complete more — they use more lethal means, e.g., hanging, firearms, jumping). (4) 70-80% of suicides occur in people NOT under mental health services — so targeting high-risk groups alone will not prevent most suicides (the 'Rose prevention paradox'). (5) The first 2 WEEKS after DISCHARGE from psychiatric hospital is the highest risk period (relative risk ~100× compared to the general population). (6) CLozapine is the only antipsychotic with FDA indication for suicide prevention. (7) Lithium is the only mood stabiliser with evidence for suicide prevention (in both bipolar and unipolar depression). Cipriani A et al. (2013, BMJ): lithium reduced risk of suicide by ~60%. The NUMBER NEEDED TO TREAT (NNT) for lithium to prevent one suicide is ~30 over 2 years.
source: NCISH Reports (University of Manchester); Cipriani A et al. (2013) Lithium and suicide; NICE CG90; NICE CG185
